title: Hello — and who are you?
goal: Greet an Indonesian correctly at any hour of the day, give your name and where you are from, ask how someone is — and discover that Indonesian builds a complete sentence without any word for "am", "is" or "are".
bekal: greet people with *selamat pagi*, *siang*, *sore* and *malam*, each at the right hour
say your name, your nationality and your city with no verb at all
turn any statement into a question just by lifting your voice at the end

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Di lift kantor
dialogs.intro: In the lift of an office tower in Jakarta, half past eight in the morning. Sarah has just arrived from Australia; Budi works on the eleventh floor.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: I'm fine too. My name is Sarah.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Saya Budi. Senang bertemu dengan Anda.
lines.id: I'm Budi. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: I Budi. happy meet with you.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Senang bertemu dengan Anda juga, Pak.
lines.id: Nice to meet you too, sir.
lines.literal: happy meet with you also, Mr.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Oh, jauh sekali! Anda orang Australia?
lines.id: Oh, that's very far! You're Australian?
lines.literal: oh, far very! you person Australia?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Yes. Are you from Jakarta, sir?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bukan, saya orang Surabaya. Tapi saya tinggal di Jakarta.
lines.id: No, I'm from Surabaya. But I live in Jakarta.
lines.literal: not, I person Surabaya. but I live at Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: I see. See you, Pak Budi!

notes: **There is no "am", "is" or "are".** Look at *Nama saya Sarah* and *Saya dari Australia*. Nothing joins the two halves; the sentence is simply "name I Sarah" and "I from Australia". This is not lazy Indonesian — it is the correct and only form. Adding a word to fill the gap is the single most common beginner mistake, and it makes a sentence wrong rather than merely clumsy.

**Apa kabar? is a ritual, not a medical enquiry.** Word for word it is "what news?", and the answer is essentially always *baik* ("good"), even on a bad day — exactly like "how are you?" in English. *Baik-baik saja* ("just fine") and *kabar baik* are equally good answers.

**Anda is the formal "you", and Indonesians barely use it in speech.** With a man old enough to be a colleague or senior, they say *Bapak* (or *Pak*) — literally "father". Sarah does exactly this in line 10: *Bapak orang Jakarta?* — "Are you from Jakarta, sir?" Unit 3 sorts the whole system out. For now: *Anda* is always safe, if a little cool.

**Bukan, not tidak, to deny a noun.** Budi says *Bukan, saya orang Surabaya* because what he is denying is the noun phrase "person of Jakarta". If Sarah had asked *Anda lapar?* ("Are you hungry?") the answer would have been *tidak*, because *lapar* is an adjective. Unit 6 makes this permanent; noticing it now is enough.

**Orang means "person", and it is how nationalities are built.** *Orang Australia* = "person Australia" = an Australian. There is no separate adjective form to learn: *orang Indonesia*, *orang Jepang*, *orang Inggris*. The same word also means "people" and turns up later as a counting word.

grammars.title: The sentence with no verb
body: Indonesian joins two nouns, or a noun and an adjective, by putting them next to each other. English needs a verb in the gap; Indonesian needs nothing.
after: ⚠️ There *is* a word *adalah* that looks like "is", and beginners fall on it with relief. Resist. It belongs to formal written definitions — *Jakarta adalah ibu kota Indonesia* ("Jakarta is the capital of Indonesia") — and in ordinary speech it sounds like a legal document. Never use it before an adjective: *Saya adalah lapar* is simply wrong.
The gift here is bigger than it looks. Nine of the sentences in this unit's exercises need no verb at all, and every one of them would need a conjugated verb in French, German or Spanish.

grammars.title: Greetings by the clock
body: Indonesian sorts greetings by the hour, not by politeness. *Selamat* literally means "safe" — the same word as in *selamat datang*, "welcome".

head: Indonesian
Say it
When
rows: Good day — 11 a.m. to about 3 p.m.
Hello — casual, and on the phone
Safe journey — said to the one leaving
Goodbye — said by the one leaving

after: 💬 In speech the *selamat* is usually dropped between people who know each other: just *Pagi!* or *Malam, Pak!*

⚠️ *Selamat malam* is a **greeting**, not a way of saying goodnight before bed. For that you need *selamat tidur*. And the pair *selamat jalan* / *selamat tinggal* is decided by who is walking away: the one who stays says *selamat jalan*, the one who leaves says *selamat tinggal*. Get it backwards and you will be gently laughed at.

sections.title: Questions without moving a single word

blocks.text: This is the second gift of the language, and it arrives on page one. To ask a yes/no question, say the statement and let your voice rise at the end. Nothing is added, nothing is reversed.

In careful or written Indonesian you may see *apakah* at the front — *Apakah Anda orang Jakarta?* It is the formal yes/no marker, roughly the job English does by inverting "you are" into "are you". You should recognise it; you rarely need to say it.

The question **words** are just as well behaved: they sit exactly where the answer would sit. *Anda dari mana?* is "you from where?", and the answer *Saya dari Australia* has the same shape with *mana* swapped for *Australia*. Nothing is fronted, nothing is inverted.

⚠️ Note *Nama Anda siapa?* — literally "your name is **who**?". Indonesian asks *siapa* ("who") about names, never *apa* ("what"). *Nama Anda apa?* is understood but sounds like you are asking what kind of object the name is.

sections.title: Ten phrases that keep you afloat

blocks.text: Not grammar — equipment. Memorise them whole today and understand their insides later.

⚠️ **Two different "please".** *Tolong* is for asking someone to do something for you (*Tolong ulangi* — "please repeat"). *Silakan* is for inviting someone to go ahead (*Silakan duduk* — "please, sit down"). Using *silakan* to ask for help sounds as odd as saying "help yourself" when you mean "help me".

The last two lines are worth more than fifty memorised words. *Tolong pelan-pelan* rescues a conversation that has run away from you, and *Apa bahasa Indonesianya?* turns everyone around you into a dictionary.
